name: CardsGame
oneLiner: A five-card draw poker engine where a model, a heuristic and a person sit at the table through the same tool boundary.
summary: A game of draw poker in which `CardsGame.Engine` has no I/O and no dependencies and is the only authority on whether a draw is legal and how strong a hand is — everything else asks it. The LLM agent gets exactly two tools, `GetHandState` and `ProposeDiscard`, and `PokerTools` is an instance class with the seat number closed over in the constructor, so there is no argument by which the model could play for someone else; the other players' cards are not in the returned object. The most interesting decision, though, is in `AgentPlayer`: after a turn it **asks the engine whether the draw actually happened**, rather than parsing the move out of the model's prose, and a rejection is an ordinary outcome carrying a reason back — three attempts and the seat stands pat. Who sits in a seat (Foundry, Azure OpenAI, a heuristic, a person) is an entry in the `PokerPlayers:<key>` section rather than code, and an unknown key falls back to the heuristic with a warning instead of throwing. Beyond the game there is `POST /simulations`: one line-up over up to 1000 hands, win rate with ties split, rejection rate, forfeits and p95 turn latency, repeatable through a seed. {{term:aspire|Aspire}} composes the lot — server, Blazor Server, console client — and it starts with no account, no key and no Docker. The one thing never done is playing even a single hand against a live model.
tests: Three test projects (Engine, Agents, Server): 102 `[Fact]`, 32 `[Theory]`, 134 `[InlineData]` and 2 `[MemberData]` expanded over the nine hand rules, so roughly 254 cases — consistent with the '250+' the README declares. The number comes from counting attributes in the sources, not from a `dotnet test` run.
ci: Three workflows. `ci.yml` has a separate `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` job, a build+test matrix on ubuntu/windows/macos with `fail-fast: false`, a CLI smoke test feeding stdin, a publish check for four RIDs and `permissions: contents: read`. `codeql.yml` has a weekly cron, but the `analyze` job is conditional, because the repository is private and has no code scanning; `release.yml` waits for a `v*` tag that has never existed.

components.name: CardsGame.AppHost i ServiceDefaults
components.description: 116 lines of shared infrastructure: {{term:otel|OTel}} self-instrumentation, health checks, service discovery and HTTP resilience, without a single domain entity. AppHost waits for the server's `/health` before letting the UI and the console client in.

components.name: CardsGame.Engine
components.description: 1,193 lines with no dependencies and no I/O: `Card` as a `readonly record struct`, nine `IHandRule` rules with separate tiebreakers, `Deck` with a real draw pile and `DrawPokerGame` as a state machine. Hand precedence follows from `HandCategory` rather than from a separate `Priority` field, which in the previous version managed to drift away from poker.

components.name: PokerTools
components.description: Two methods with `[Description]` attributes and nothing else. The class is an instance class holding the seat number from its constructor, so the model's tool surface is {{term:hermetyczny|sealed off}} from the other players at the level of the type, not of validation.

components.name: AgentPlayer i PokerAgentFactory
components.description: A turn loop with a budget of three attempts and verification on the engine's side instead of parsing the model's reply. The factory has two paths, because `AIProjectClient.AsAIAgent` builds an `AIAgent` bypassing the intermediate `IChatClient`.

components.name: PokerPlayerFactory
components.description: The only place that decides what fills a given chair — Foundry, Azure OpenAI, a heuristic or a person — on the basis of configuration. A missing key degrades to the heuristic with a warning, so a fresh clone plays without any account at all.

components.name: SimulationRunner
components.description: A comparison harness: hands run sequentially, because parallelism would falsify the latency of the model seats, ties are split so that win rate sums to one, p95 by the nearest-rank method. A human seat is rejected, because there is nobody to answer.

components.name: HumanDrawGate
components.description: A `TaskCompletionSource` with `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`, so that the rest of the hand does not finish inline on the HTTP request thread. It carries the engine's `RejectionReason` back to the seat's view, so a person gets the same message as a model.

components.name: ScriptedAgent
components.description: An `AIAgent` stub playing back a planned sequence of tool calls. It gives determinism in the retry and forfeit tests without a network or an Azure subscription, including the case of an agent that never works.

overlaps.reason: The same pattern carried over to another game: `HumanMoveGate` against `HumanDrawGate`, `ChessMetrics` against `GameMetrics`, a tool boundary tied to one side. Comments in the code refer to ChessMas by name.
Also a perfect-information game driven by models, with move validation on the engine's side instead of trust in the model's output.
`SimulationRunner` is in effect an agent benchmark: win rate, rejection rate, forfeits and latency under a repeatable seed. That one measures the same things on tasks, this one on hands.
The repository runs on `Microsoft.Agents.AI` 1.15.0 and `.Foundry`, that is on exactly the API the book describes — and on the version the book has not yet caught up with.
The src/tests layout, the bare xunit and the separation of server DTOs from UI DTOs are copied from there; the changelog and the comments say so outright.

product: No buyer, and there is no point pretending otherwise. This is an {{term:evidence|evidence}} project: it shows how to shut a language model inside a boundary that cannot be talked around, and how to measure the quality of play rather than whether HTTP returned 200. The simulation runner comes closest to being useful, but until a live model has been run through it, there is not a single number in it to publish. The portfolio value is real, the product value zero.
gaps: **The model seats have never played against a live Foundry or Azure OpenAI deployment.** The README says so honestly, but it means the repository's main claim has not a single measurement with a real model behind it — only the construction tests and `ScriptedAgent` cover it.
The sample simulation result in the README is four copies of the heuristic playing each other. It is a demonstration of the mechanics served in the place where the reader expects a result.
The repository is private, so the `analyze` job in `codeql.yml` is conditional and the analysis never runs. The CodeQL badge in the README therefore describes a workflow that does nothing.
Zero git tags against a fully written `release.yml` — no CLI artefact has ever been produced, and the README still says 'Not yet released'.

No containerisation, no authentication and no persistence; `HandRegistry` keeps 200 hands in memory. All three are listed in the 'Deliberately not done' section, so this is deliberate debt, not debt that was missed.
next: Stand up one Foundry deployment and run a few hundred hands of a model-against-three-heuristics line-up. **Keep the raw event streams, not just the summary rows** — repeating the run only to recover the traces costs the same again.
Put that result in the README in place of the four heuristics, and mark plainly what still has not been measured.
Settle the name: the directory is `cards-game`, while the badge, the `git clone` and the URL in the README point at `konradcinkusz/CardsGame`. Two names for one project in one README.
Tag `v0.1.0`, so that `release.yml` stops being a declaration, and while you are there check how much the binaries really weigh without trimming.
Open the repository or turn on code scanning — otherwise remove the CodeQL badge, because it promises a check that is not there.
highlights: The changelog records **seven real correctness bugs** from the previous version, among them a parser registering three of the nine rules (a royal flush reported as `Flush`) and `Rank.Ace` with a value of 0, which made an ace-high straight undetectable. That is rare: a repository that publishes its own domain mistakes instead of quietly rewriting them.

`PokerTools` is an instance class and closes over the seat number in its constructor, and the other players' cards never reach the returned object. The boundary is a property of the type, not a condition in a validator.
After a turn `AgentPlayer` asks the engine whether the draw actually happened, rather than parsing the move out of the model's prose; three rejections with a reason returned and the seat stands pat.

CI builds and tests on ubuntu, windows and macos, checks formatting in a separate job, runs a CLI smoke test feeding stdin and a publish check for four RIDs. `TreatWarningsAsErrors` is on globally in `Directory.Build.props`.
Roughly 254 test cases with no network and no credentials — every seat at the table is a heuristic or a `ScriptedAgent`, including an agent proposing an illegal draw and an agent that never works.
risks: Name collision: the directory is `cards-game`, while the README, the CI badge and the `git clone` command point at `https://github.com/konradcinkusz/CardsGame.git`.
`FluentAssertions` was removed on purpose, because from version 8 it carries Xceed's proprietary licence. An automatic Dependabot bump could put it back into an MIT project with no signal at all.

The pinning runs ahead (Aspire 13.4.6, `Microsoft.Agents.AI` 1.15.0, SDK 10.0.100 with `rollForward latestMinor`) — without a periodic check against NuGet it will go stale faster than the project gets picked up again.
headline: The boundary holds and is tested; no live model has played a single hand
